title: English as a Second Language

jokes.text: Dean announces soothing nature sounds over the PA to reduce finals stress, then immediately blares a 'babbling brook'
jokes.setup: Dean sympathetically acknowledges his PA announcements are stressful and promises relief via nature sounds
jokes.punchline: He then blares a babbling brook over the PA, which is exactly as jarring and disruptive as his normal announcements
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton obliviousness — his self-awareness about being annoying doesn't translate into actually being less annoying. The character integration is strong because only Dean would think this was helpful. Solid cold-open joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Remember when I said Avatar was overrated? And you all just... left me hanging on that?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I needed support! But no, suddenly everyone's a Cameron apologist.

jokes.text: Will anyone back me up if I say this is ridiculous, or is it gonna be another avatar situation?
jokes.setup: The babbling brook PA announcement is clearly absurd; Jeff wants to voice dissent
jokes.punchline: His hesitation implies the group has previously failed to back him up when criticizing something popular (Avatar), making his contrarianism a known losing battle
jokes.explanation: Very economical — the Avatar reference does triple duty: it's a topical jab, it characterizes Jeff as a contrarian who's been burned before, and it characterizes the group as people who go along with popular things. 'Avatar situation' is a genuinely quotable coinage.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Nerd alert.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Spoiler alert.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Alert nerd.

jokes.text: "Spoiler alert." / "You mean 'nerd alert.'" / "Alert nerd."
jokes.setup: Abed reveals he records every class; someone calls it a 'spoiler alert'
jokes.punchline: Troy corrects it to 'nerd alert'; Britta offers the anagram-ish non-correction 'alert nerd,' which is both useless and confident
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke in six words. Each beat escalates absurdly: Abed's deadpan 'spoiler alert,' Troy's sensible correction, and Britta's hilariously meaningless rearrangement that she delivers with apparent satisfaction. Tight, character-specific, and genuinely clever in its escalating wrongness.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I don't need to understand Spanish. My neighbors hate me in English just fine.

jokes.text: Jeff's reason for not wanting to continue Spanish: 'I know the family downstairs hates me. I don't need to understand why.'
jokes.setup: Britta argues Spanish has value beyond academic credit
jokes.punchline: Jeff's counterargument reveals his precise, selfish calculus — he has already internalized that his neighbors hate him and has decided ignorance is preferable
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. It's a perfect encapsulation of Jeff's character — selfish, self-aware, and weirdly logical about his own antisocial behavior. The specificity ('the family downstairs') makes it feel lived-in rather than generic. High quotability because it's a universal sentiment expressed with perfect precision. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Fine. I'll be in Spanish 103 next semester. Without you.

jokes.text: Annie tells Jeff he'll be lonely next fall when his cool-guy attitude fails him, then reveals the Spanish 103 class is Monday through Friday at 6:00 AM
jokes.setup: Annie tells Jeff his cool-guy independence will get lonely — implying emotional consequences
jokes.punchline: The practical punchline is that the class she'd be taking (Spanish 103) is at 6:00 AM, which horrifies Jeff more than the loneliness argument
jokes.explanation: A clean two-beat joke. Annie's emotional argument leads us to expect a dramatic response from Jeff; instead, the reveal is purely practical. Jeff's horror at '6:00...' is a reaction beat that sells it. Competent but not outstanding.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Spanish 103 meets at 7 AM.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: 7 AM? That's... that's when I'm usually just falling asleep.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not a morning person, Annie. I'm a 'sleep until noon and emerge as a fully formed human' person.

jokes.text: "I'm still trying to forget what I learned about that subject." / "Go, girl." / "You just 'go girled' yourself."
jokes.setup: Shirley enthusiastically endorses anthropology as 'the study of man'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's self-deprecating quip leads Shirley to 'go girl' him, which Jeff immediately turns back on her — she's endorsed a man's self-pity
jokes.explanation: Three-beat exchange with a satisfying loop: Jeff sets up self-deprecation, Shirley accidentally endorses it with 'go girl,' and Jeff weaponizes Shirley's own phrase against her. Fast, character-consistent, and structurally clean.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Go, girl!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, you just said 'go, girl' to yourself about yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's so meta.

jokes.text: Pierce says he has 'one unmovable appointment: May 23rd, 2013 — to buy a flying car'
jokes.setup: Annie asks Pierce about planning ahead; the expectation is a mundane life milestone
jokes.punchline: Pierce's unmovable appointment is to buy a flying car — revealing both his absurd optimism and his detachment from reality. Annie's flat 'To buy a flying car?' sells it.
jokes.explanation: Good Pierce joke — the specific date (2013) makes it feel like he's earnestly planned this, which makes it funnier than if it were vague. Annie's echo-punchline delivery is key to landing it.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: May 23rd, 2013? That's so far away. What is it, some kind of intergalactic meeting?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's my colonoscopy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Jeff describes his May 2013 appointment as 'a table for one at Morty's Steakhouse where I will celebrate becoming a lawyer again' — then tells the group not to make a 'full load' joke
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining his serious four-year plan to become a lawyer again
jokes.punchline: He preemptively says 'Don't' before the words 'full load' — interrupting his own speech to police the group's juvenile humor, which is funnier than any actual dirty joke would have been
jokes.explanation: A meta joke that works because Jeff's preemptive 'Don't' is funnier than any dirty joke the writers could have put in the other characters' mouths. The restraint IS the joke. Strong structure — setup is straight-faced, the interruption reframes everything, and the resumption ('a full load of classes every year') plays it completely straight.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta, you can't just dismiss friendship like that. Your parents named you Britta. That's what happens when hippies have children.

jokes.text: Jeff accuses Annie of naming her parents pot-smokers by saying 'It's obvious from your name your parents smoked pot.'
jokes.setup: Britta says the group will still be friends without a shared class
jokes.punchline: Jeff dismisses her optimism by insulting her name as a pot-smoker giveaway — which is also a subtle callback to Britta's established hippie-adjacent background
jokes.explanation: A casual Jeff burn that works because it's specific and character-integrated. The name 'Britta' genuinely does sound like a hippie-parent name choice, so the joke has a logic to it. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: ¡Hola, amigos!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You are all un-believable.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'All right, well, I haven't said a single word in this entire conversation, and I find that outrageous.'
jokes.setup: The group has been having a long, emotionally significant conversation about their future
jokes.punchline: Pierce has been silent the entire time and his complaint is not that he was ignored, but that he HIMSELF hasn't said anything — a perfect expression of his oblivious self-centeredness
jokes.explanation: Superb Pierce joke. The grammar of his complaint is the entire joke — 'I haven't said a single word' means he's outraged at himself, not at being excluded. It's a precise, character-specific absurdity that couldn't belong to anyone else in the ensemble. Earns its 8+ for character integration alone.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Pierce, close the door from inside.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: From inside?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No, no, from outside. You'll be outside when you close it.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: "Hola, el losers."
jokes.setup: Chang enters the study room and greets the group
jokes.punchline: His Spanish greeting is grammatically wrong ("el losers" misuses the definite article) — ironic given he's a Spanish teacher
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective piece of dramatic irony — Chang's bad Spanish foreshadows his fraudulence. Funnier on rewatch when you know he's been faking it. The character integration is excellent; this joke only works because of who Chang is.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, your degree is fake?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's not fake, it's... alternative.

jokes.text: Chang asks Jeff to close the door, Pierce says 'Gracias' and closes it from inside — Chang then says 'Other side of the door.'
jokes.setup: Chang asks for privacy with Jeff and tells Pierce to close the door
jokes.punchline: Pierce closes it from inside, trapping himself in the conversation — then has to be redirected to the other side
jokes.explanation: A clean physical bit — Pierce's 'Gracias' shows he understood the Spanish but not the intent. The beat-pause before 'Other side of the door' lands it. Competent visual/physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I have two questions.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: First, what is this? Second, why is this? Third, how dare you?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I have one question.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What were you thinking? And why would you do that?

jokes.text: Chang corrects Jeff's vocabulary: 'I prefer the term better than real.' Jeff asks three questions calling it 'two questions' — Chang calls him out: 'One question. Where did you learn to count questions?'
jokes.setup: Jeff says he has 'two questions' and then asks three, then immediately asks another question about Chang needing a fake degree
jokes.punchline: Chang catches him in the counting error mid-sentence and uses the same construction ('one question, where did you learn to count?') to point it out
jokes.explanation: Formally elegant — Chang uses the same 'x questions' structure to catch Jeff's counting error, turning Jeff's rhetorical device against him. The structural mirroring is satisfying and unexpected. Also includes the nice opener of Chang's 'better than real' euphemism for a fake degree.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A key-tar? What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's a keyboard that you wear like a guitar. It's awesome.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That sounds like the worst thing ever invented.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if you had any musical talent, you'd understand!

jokes.text: Chang: 'The world wasn't ready for an Asian man on key-tar.' Jeff: 'Did you say key-tar or did you just pronounce guitar like a hillbilly?'
jokes.setup: Chang explains his backstory — he was in a band that could've been huge
jokes.punchline: Jeff's first question is not about the band but about whether 'key-tar' is a real instrument or a mispronunciation — genuinely funny misunderstanding that also characterizes Jeff's cultural blind spots
jokes.explanation: Jeff's 'hillbilly' read on key-tar is a genuinely funny misunderstanding. 'The world wasn't ready for an Asian man on key-tar' is also a funny standalone sentiment — Chang's self-aggrandizing victimhood narrative is perfectly absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys get tips? I've been bagging groceries wrong my whole life.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yeah man, five bucks an hour plus tips.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh my God. How much have I not tipped you?

jokes.text: Jeff: "Did you say 'key-tar' or did you just pronounce guitar like a hillbilly?"
jokes.setup: Chang mentions key-tar
jokes.punchline: Jeff doesn't know what a key-tar is and assumes it's Chang mispronouncing 'guitar' in a rural accent
jokes.explanation: Jeff's condescension applied to something he doesn't know about is a great character beat. The 'hillbilly' specification is specific enough to be funny rather than generic. Chang's irritated correction ('Get with the times, man') adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I went from bagging groceries to teaching Spanish at a community college. Now I use the Spanish I learned from children's TV shows to teach college students.

jokes.text: Jeff's reaction to Chang's tip-the-bag-boy confusion: 'I'm supposed to tip my bag boy?'
jokes.setup: Chang says he was bagging groceries for $5/hour 'plus tips' and Jeff is shocked
jokes.punchline: Jeff's shock isn't about Chang's humiliation — it's about the revelation that you can tip your bag boy, exposing Jeff's oblivious upper-class insularity
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-deployed character beat. Jeff's obliviousness to tipping service workers is very on-brand — his privileged myopia is played as innocently as possible, which is funnier than making him deliberately callous.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It was just the chair! The chair made that noise!

jokes.text: Chang says 'I faked my way into a job as a Spanish teacher at a community college relying on phrases from Sesame Street.' Jeff's reaction beat — a long pause before: 'That was the chair. Good.'
jokes.setup: Chang reveals his entire career as a Spanish teacher was based on Sesame Street phrases
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response is apparently an audible reaction (gas, squeak, etc.) which he attributes to 'the chair' — his attempt to maintain composure after a shocking revelation fails hilariously
jokes.explanation: The 'that was the chair' gag works because it's both a physical comedy inference (Jeff made an involuntary sound) and a classic deflection. The deadpan 'Good' after is the right choice — Jeff collecting himself is funnier than any verbal response to Chang's bombshell.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He said, 'I'm going to hurt you,' and then he added this weird thing about a chair.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: The chair knows what it did.

jokes.text: Dean announces bad news and then corrects himself: 'Well, it's actually bad news for the older people as well.'
jokes.setup: Dean begins to announce news by saying 'I have some bad news for you kids'
jokes.punchline: He pauses to realize that bad news isn't just for kids and extends the condolence to the adults — revealing his social awkwardness through over-literal correction
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean micro-beat — his compulsive correction of an innocent idiom ('bad news for you kids') is perfectly Dean. The timing-dependent delivery means it works better on screen than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, Chang died? Again? Oh my God, I can't go through this again. The last time he 'died,' I had to identify the body. Do you know what that does to a person?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: And then he just showed up at school like nothing happened! I had already picked out flowers and written a eulogy!

jokes.text: On hearing Chang left, Britta asks: 'He's not faking his death again, is he? Because I can't handle that roller coaster. First he's alive. And then we're happy. And then he's alive again and...'
jokes.setup: Dean announces Chang is gone
jokes.punchline: Britta implies Chang has previously faked his death more than once — a callback to unseen prior events — and her description of the emotional rollercoaster is so earnest it becomes absurd
jokes.explanation: Funny because it implies a whole unshown history of Chang faking his death repeatedly, and Britta's sincere trauma about it is characterful. The trailing off ('...and then he's alive again and...') perfectly implies exhaustion without overstating it.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, we discovered Chang's credentials were forged when we cross-referenced them with the actual schools. It was really quite simple once we looked into it.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The important thing is, we need to be careful about making assumptions based on appearance. I mean, you can't just profile someone because they... well, because they look a certain way.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Although, in this case, we probably should have seen it coming from a mile away. We really dropped the ball on that one.

jokes.text: Dean: 'Word of advice — if an Asian man says he's a Spanish teacher, it's not racist to ask for proof. You ignore your mother's voice and get right into that horse's mouth.'
jokes.setup: Dean is giving the group advice about being skeptical of Chang's credentials
jokes.punchline: His advice is delivered as wisdom but is itself a casually racist heuristic — 'if an Asian man says he's a Spanish teacher' — wrapped in a mangled idiom ('get right into that horse's mouth')
jokes.explanation: The Dean dispensing advice that is itself the problem is classic Dean Pelton. The mangled idiom ('get into that horse's mouth' instead of 'straight from the horse's mouth') adds a layer of incompetence to the casual prejudice, which is the right tone for this character.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: This is just like when I negotiated that trade agreement with the Guatemalan Minister of Commerce.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Except he was actually listening to me.

jokes.text: Dr. Escodera responds to everything in Spanish; Jeff listens and says 'Listen to this back and forth. It's like I'm at an embassy.'
jokes.setup: The new Spanish teacher responds exclusively in Spanish to the class
jokes.punchline: Jeff frames a Spanish class being conducted in Spanish as an exotic and confusing experience — the joke is that he's apparently never considered this a possibility
jokes.explanation: 'Like I'm at an embassy' is a funny specific — Jeff reaches for a formal, diplomatic context rather than 'like I'm in Mexico' or something obvious. It tells you something about Jeff's frame of reference (fancy, cosmopolitan) while also being perfectly absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'll have a venti caramel macchiato.

jokes.text: Jeff asks what's on the final in English; Dr. Escodera responds 'En español, por favor'; Jeff: 'I know it's in Spanish, dummy. I'm just saying what chapters?'
jokes.setup: Dr. Escodera instructs students to speak in Spanish
jokes.punchline: Jeff misreads her instruction — she meant 'ask me in Spanish' but he thinks she's clarifying the language of the exam — and then calls her 'dummy' for it
jokes.explanation: The misunderstanding is sharp — Jeff's confident 'I know it's in Spanish, dummy' is funnier than if he'd been confused. His arrogance about being wrong is the character-specific element. Calling the teacher 'dummy' caps it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dios mío!

jokes.text: Pierce mishears 'veinte' (twenty, as in the number of chapters) and says 'Oh, I know that one — she wants a large coffee.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Escodera says 'veinte' (twenty) in response to what chapters the final covers
jokes.punchline: Pierce conflates 'veinte' with 'venti' (Starbucks size), revealing both his incompetence in Spanish and his oblivious consumer brain
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed: the confusion is plausible (the words really do sound similar), it's character-specific (Pierce's mind goes to Starbucks), and it's delivered with Pierce's signature confidence. The specific detail of 'large coffee' rather than just 'Starbucks' makes it land better.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dr. Escodera should focus on being a doctor. You can't be good at two things.

jokes.text: "Veinte." / "I know that one. She wants a large coffee."
jokes.setup: Dr. Escodera says 'veinte' (twenty, as in all twenty chapters)
jokes.punchline: Pierce confidently announces he knows this word — but thinks it means a large coffee (Starbucks 'venti')
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The Starbucks/Spanish confusion is both culturally specific and perfectly Pierce: he knows a vaguely Spanish-sounding word from his coffee order and applies it with total confidence. It's funny, structurally tight, characterizes Pierce's brand of confident ignorance, and works on a wordplay level. The specificity (not just 'coffee' but 'large coffee') makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's a 2004 Honda Civic. I can tell by the pitch.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How is that even possible?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I have a gift.

jokes.text: "El crappo."
jokes.setup: Dr. Escodera reveals the final will cover the entire textbook
jokes.punchline: Jeff's one-word reaction is delivered in mock-Spanish, suggesting he's already absorbing the language in the worst possible way
jokes.explanation: A perfect economy joke — two words, bilingual reaction. The faux-Spanish suffix on an English expletive captures the absurdity of their situation. Quick, effective, very Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang! What are you doing to my car?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Relax, I'm wearing a seatbelt.

jokes.text: Shirley in confessional: 'I couldn't understand a word Dr. Escodera was saying. And why is she teaching Spanish if she's a doctor? Go cure something.'
jokes.setup: Shirley reflects on the new Spanish teacher who is apparently a PhD
jokes.punchline: Shirley conflates 'Doctor' (academic) with 'Doctor' (medical) and demands she go cure diseases instead — a perfect expression of Shirley's pragmatic, unfiltered worldview
jokes.explanation: 'Go cure something' is a perfect Shirley line — blunt, slightly unreasonable, completely sincere. The confusion between academic and medical doctorate is relatable but filtered through Shirley's specific no-nonsense personality. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! You don't understand. Jeff and I are working on a musical collaboration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We are not—

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's called 'Kick Me in the Face: A Love Story.' I write, he interprets through interpretive violence.

jokes.text: Troy reveals he was on the roof for the Fourth of July, and when Jeff's car alarm goes off he identifies it as 'a brand-new Lexus' — then corrects himself: 'Yours is a 2002. That's the year I heard it.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is alarmed that someone trashed his car; Troy seems to helpfully identify the alarm sound
jokes.punchline: Troy not only recognizes Jeff's specific Lexus by its alarm sound but can date the model year — revealing an absurdly specific knowledge of Jeff's car that implies obsessive surveillance
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I know the brand' to 'I know the model year by ear' is very funny — it's the specificity that elevates this. Troy's casual delivery of encyclopedic knowledge about Jeff's car implies a whole unexamined parasocial dynamic. Character-specific and original.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: My teaching methods are unconventional, but they work. I connect with students on a deeper level.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang, what is that sound? That creaking noise that happens every time you sit down?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I have a medical condition. My spine makes sounds when I move. It's called spinal stenosis.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So all those mysterious chair sounds in class...

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: That's just me, Jeff. That's just me.

jokes.text: Chang confronts Jeff wearing protective goggles while destroying his car. 'You're wearing protective goggles to destroy my car?' Chang: 'Safety first!'
jokes.setup: Chang is caught vandalizing Jeff's car
jokes.punchline: Chang's only defense is that he's being safe about it — the responsible application of safety protocols to vandalism is perfectly absurd
jokes.explanation: 'Safety first' as a response to being caught committing vandalism is a great absurdist beat. Chang's chaotic energy channeled through earnest safety compliance is a funny character contradiction.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Plumber? A plumber. Me? A plumber. Could I be... a plumber?

jokes.text: Chang: 'Tell me who did it so I can murder your face!'
jokes.setup: Jeff denies turning Chang in; Chang demands to know who did
jokes.punchline: 'Murder your face' is a distinctive, slightly surreal threat that's specific enough to be funny — murdering a face rather than a person
jokes.explanation: Chang's idiosyncratic violent threats are part of his character's voice. 'Murder your face' is a funny specificity but it's a fairly common type of surreal threat in comedy of this era. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? What was that 'hmm'? That sounded suspicious.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, the ability to curl your tongue is a dominant genetic trait. Watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: See? I can curl mine. That means I'm genetically superior.

jokes.text: Jeff and Chang's confrontation is interrupted by Pierce, who claims they're 'writing a song for the battle of bands'
jokes.setup: Chang and Jeff are physically fighting in a parking lot
jokes.punchline: Pierce's cover story — that they're writing a song for a battle of bands — is so non-sequitur that it only works as misdirection for someone as oblivious as the person he's trying to fool
jokes.explanation: A quick beat that earns a mild laugh from Pierce's absurd cover story. It's not especially crafted — the humor is entirely in the incongruity. Competent filler.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You betrayed Chang because deep down, you knew that no matter what you did, you'd never be as physically developed as the other girls in your class. So you figured, why not just burn it all down?

jokes.text: Chang, departing: 'Good luck passing your exam, Winger. At one point, I was teaching you Klingon!'
jokes.setup: Chang is leaving, throwing parting shots at Jeff about being screwed on his exam
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Chang at some point taught the class Klingon instead of Spanish is a devastating retroactive absurdity — the entire semester's curriculum may have been fictional
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'At one point, I was teaching you Klingon' is delivered as a parting shot but lands as a horrifying revelation about everything the audience thought they knew. The specificity of Klingon (not 'gibberish' or 'pig latin' but an actual constructed alien language) is perfect. It's both a Chang character joke and a retroactive deconstruction of the entire season's Spanish class. Earns 8+ comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're like a golden retriever in a cardigan.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Jeff's comeback to Chang: 'Yeah? Why don't you tell that to your really weird-sounding magical chair?' Chang: 'I have a condition!'
jokes.setup: Jeff is retorting to Chang's Klingon insult; this references the earlier 'that was the chair' gag
jokes.punchline: Chang's indignant 'I have a condition!' confirms the earlier ambiguous sound was indeed him, not the chair — escalating the original joke and vindicating Jeff's suspicion
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'that was the chair' pays off with Chang's 'I have a condition!' — confirming what we suspected. Jeff's formulation ('really weird-sounding magical chair') is a funny way to frame the callback. The payoff justifies the original setup.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, I have an idea. What if Annie were a guy? Then we could all hit her.

jokes.text: Following 'I have a condition!', there is an implied physical comedy sequence ending with 'Oh. I'm peeing. I'm peeing. I'm peeing.'
jokes.setup: Chang is in an agitated state confronting Jeff
jokes.punchline: Chang involuntarily urinates — apparently a symptom of his 'condition' — and narrates it in real time with panicked repetition
jokes.explanation: Bodily humor that's elevated slightly by its connection to the 'condition' callback. The triple repetition of 'I'm peeing' as a panic reaction is funnier than a single exclamation would be. Not high-craft but delivers on audience expectation. The gap between 'I have a condition' and this payoff is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You know what? I am so angry right now, I just want to punch you in the face! But I can't, because I'm a Christian woman and society says that's not ladylike. So instead I'm going to stand here and simmer, and you're going to have to live with the knowledge that you made Shirley Bennett want to commit violence!

jokes.text: Plumber's climactic pitch: 'You could be a plumber!' delivered as if it's the greatest destiny imaginable
jokes.setup: The plumber has built up Troy's gift and talked about toilets and sinks as 'real things, things that matter'
jokes.punchline: The triumphant reveal of Troy's destiny — 'You could be a PLUMBER!' — is played with the gravity of a superhero origin story, making the mundaneness of the actual destiny the entire joke
jokes.explanation: The joke works as a genre parody of the 'you have a gift, kid' mentor speech. The plumber's sincerity is not diminished by the mundaneness of plumbing — if anything his absolute conviction makes it funnier. The repetition ('You could be a plumber' again at 11:09) underlines it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: She's going to cry now. Not because she's sad, but because she knows it'll make us feel bad and stop criticizing her. She'll do the lip quiver first, then the eyes will get watery. She might even do a little shoulder shake for emphasis.

jokes.text: Second beat of 'You could be a plumber' — plumber says it again, quietly, to himself, as if it's the most beautiful thing he's ever said
jokes.setup: The plumber just delivered 'You could be a plumber!' as a triumphant revelation
jokes.punchline: He repeats it softly, as if savoring it — suggesting this moment means as much to him as it supposedly should to Troy
jokes.explanation: The soft second repetition is a perfect anti-climactic button. The plumber re-experiencing his own speech with private wonder is funny in a subtle way. Good economy — no words added, just the same phrase with new emotional weight.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Close your eyes. Everyone, close your eyes now.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie's emotional manipulation is like the Ark of the Covenant. If you look directly at it, you die.

jokes.text: Troy's response to being told he could be a plumber: 'I'm gonna be sophisticated and have no job, or a job that looks from a distance like I do nothing.'
jokes.setup: The plumber has made an earnest case for Troy becoming a plumber
jokes.punchline: Troy's aspirational alternative to plumbing is 'sophisticated and have no job' — a perfect articulation of a certain type of young man's ambitions, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'A job that looks from a distance like I do nothing' is one of the best Troy lines in the episode. It's both a specific, quotable aspiration and a perfect character portrait — Troy's earnest delivery of a deeply impractical life plan. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, here's what we do. Whenever Annie tries to manipulate us emotionally, just imagine her as an unattractive middle-aged actor.

jokes.text: Troy tells the plumber: 'Troy, I know you could be a plumber.' The plumber's speech about 'toilets and sinks — real things!' is undercut by Troy's response.
jokes.setup: Plumber gives an earnest speech about toilets and sinks being 'real things, things people always need'
jokes.punchline: Troy counters with a vision of himself being sophisticated and idle — the total philosophical opposition, delivered without irony
jokes.explanation: This is the structural context for Joke #35 — the plumber's sincere pitch being rebuffed. Counted separately as the 'toilets and sinks' speech has its own comedic energy, particularly 'this is a life, kid — a real one.' The parody of mentor-movie gravitas is consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to give you a passionate analysis of a movie I haven't seen.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Inception. It's about a guy who goes into people's dreams. It's brilliant because... it's confusing. And confusion is just another word for smart.

jokes.text: Jeff says 'Permission to treat the witness as hostile.' The Dean-like character says 'I'll allow it.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is about to cross-examine Annie about whether she informed on Chang
jokes.punchline: The courtroom language in a study room is absurd; someone actually granting the permission makes it more absurd by implying they have judicial authority
jokes.explanation: Jeff's former-lawyer schtick being deployed in casual social situations is a consistent joke. 'I'll allow it' from someone with no judicial authority is a perfect absurdist addition. The beat works.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I tried that. I met a guy in rehab who said we'd stay in touch. He was in for eating disorders and narcissism, which is a weird combination. Anyway, he's dead now.

jokes.text: Jeff's accusation escalates to: 'You are insecure — because you didn't get hot until after high school.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is building a case that Annie's manipulation stems from deep insecurity
jokes.punchline: The final, specific insult — that she was unattractive in high school and her attachment to the group stems from still being unused to having friends — is delivered as an analytical observation, not a meanness, which makes it simultaneously crueler and funnier
jokes.explanation: One of the show's darker comedy beats — Jeff's psychological insight deployed as a weapon. 'You didn't get hot until after high school' is both an insult and an explanation, and the fact that it's demonstrably accurate (the whole group immediately accepts it) makes it sting and land simultaneously. High character integration for both Jeff and Annie.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: As part of our new soothing nature sounds policy, we'll be playing calming forest ambiances throughout the campus.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: However, I've discovered that violent animal death sounds are actually much more effective for stress relief.

jokes.text: After Jeff says Annie 'didn't get hot until after high school,' Abed simply says: 'That's true.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has delivered a psychologically cutting observation about Annie's insecurity
jokes.punchline: Abed confirms it as a matter of fact, with zero social awareness that this is not a helpful thing to say
jokes.explanation: Two words, perfect character integration. Abed's confirmation is devastating to Annie and funny to the audience because it treats Jeff's cruelty as an empirical observation requiring verification. Only Abed would do this. Economy score near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We need to wake up Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Has anyone considered the legal liability if we do this wrong?

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Someone make her a dude so I can punch her.'
jokes.setup: Annie has confessed and the group is reacting with anger
jokes.punchline: Pierce's immediate instinct is violence but he's restrained by his (nominally) chivalric code — so he outsources the gender change requirement to others
jokes.explanation: Very Pierce — his frustration is genuine but his code of chivalry creates an absurd logical impasse. The phrasing 'make her a dude so I can punch her' is funny because it treats gender as a practical obstacle to violence rather than an inherent value. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Troy, listen to me. When you're in love, you have to be willing to make sacrifices. You have to say things like, 'I hope you disappear so I can be alone with my thoughts and my premium cable subscriptions.'

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That doesn't sound right.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's not. I'm paraphrasing Ryan Gosling.

jokes.text: "Maybe not too cool, maybe just, you know, not psycho enough." / "Yeah, a little crazy." / "You're a psycho."
jokes.setup: Annie defends her actions as necessary; the group pushes back
jokes.punchline: The group's characterization of Annie escalates from 'maybe psycho' to 'a little crazy' to the blunt 'You're a psycho' — consensus reached through escalation
jokes.explanation: A quick escalation joke that works through accumulation. Each character ratchets up the diagnosis, with Shirley landing the definitive 'You're a psycho.' Functional group dynamics joke.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That speech is from a movie.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well, that movie sounds awful and nobody should watch it.

jokes.text: Jeff predicts Annie is about to 'make the Disney face' — lip quivering, eyes fluttering but never actually closing — and tells people not to feel sorry for her
jokes.setup: Annie is visibly emotional after being exposed
jokes.punchline: Jeff narrates the specific mechanics of Annie's manipulation in real time — 'her lip is gonna quiver and her eyes will flutter, but they won't ever actually close' — as if reading stage directions, making her emotional response feel performative
jokes.explanation: 'The Disney face' as a named, specific character behavior — with technical stage-direction specificity — is excellent writing. Jeff commentating on Annie's emotional manipulation in real-time while it's happening is both characterful and structurally inventive. The detail 'they won't ever actually close' is what elevates this from a good joke to a great one. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Guys, we don't need to take this exam. We can just walk out right now.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I know I'm not the most popular person in this class, but I'm asking you to trust me.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We can do this together. We're a team!

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Who are you?

jokes.text: Jeff instructs everyone to close their eyes to avoid Annie's manipulative expression; Abed says: 'Oh, don't worry about me. I can only connect with people through... movies.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to protect the group from Annie's emotional manipulation
jokes.punchline: Abed opts out not because he's strong, but because he's socially disconnected by design — he processes human emotion through cinema, not direct experience
jokes.explanation: Abed's self-description ('I can only connect with people through movies') is both a joke and a genuinely poignant character truth. The slight pause before 'movies' (suggested by the ellipsis) makes it land as self-aware melancholy rather than just a quirk gag. Extremely high character integration — this is THE Abed sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well, that's because the Lord works in mysterious ways, and sometimes He uses the stars to send us messages about our suffering.

jokes.text: Jeff shouts 'She's the ark of the covenant!' to prevent people from looking at Annie
jokes.setup: Jeff is desperately trying to keep the group from succumbing to Annie's emotional appeal
jokes.punchline: He invokes the Raiders of the Lost Ark trope — 'don't look at it or it'll melt your face' — applied to Annie's emotional expression
jokes.explanation: A reference-dependent joke that works because the Raiders connection is intuitive — 'don't look directly at the thing that will destroy you.' The escalation of Annie from 'the Disney face' to 'the ark of the covenant' is good escalation within the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I was giving her music education! I was teaching her about sampling!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Ahhhhhhh!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: See? She's learning!

jokes.text: Jeff's rebuttal to Annie: 'Did the Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants poison each other's food so they'd be too sick to leave? No! I've never seen it, but I'm pretty sure they just mailed each other pants!'
jokes.setup: Annie defends her actions as keeping the group together
jokes.punchline: Jeff's counterexample (the Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants) is undermined by his admission that he's never seen it, yet he delivers his summary ('they mailed each other pants!') with absolute conviction
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is elegant: Jeff begins with a rhetorical question implying he knows the film, undercuts himself with 'I've never seen it,' then delivers a summary ('they mailed each other pants!') with the conviction of someone who definitely has. The specificity of 'pants' landing as the climactic word is perfect. The joke also characterizes Jeff (dismissive of female-coded media) while being genuinely funny. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You don't need to change to mature.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, that outfit makes you look like a flight attendant who got fired for being too slutty.

jokes.text: Jeff instructs the group: 'Nobody even think about going after her. That's what she wants. More personal drama so we fail the exam and stay in Spanish forever. We have to beat her.'
jokes.setup: Annie has run out crying after being accused
jokes.punchline: Jeff frames Annie's emotional breakdown as a calculated strategic move — which is both a funny paranoid read of the situation and a Jeff-specific way of processing emotions (through competition)
jokes.explanation: Jeff's reflexive competitive framing of everything — including someone else's emotional crisis — is a consistent character note. 'We have to beat her' as a response to a friend crying is darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So what do you think? Do I look mature?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You look like a woman who just discovered her dad's credit card.

jokes.text: Jeff says 'Don't mention her' — everyone agrees — then immediately: 'Does anybody know how to study?' followed by 'Annie usually—' and Jeff: 'Whose side are you on?'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just declared they will not think about Annie
jokes.punchline: The group immediately reveals their complete dependence on Annie for the very activity they're doing — someone starts to say her name and Jeff acts as if it's a betrayal
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured — the irony of declaring Annie irrelevant while immediately revealing total dependence on her is clean. 'Whose side are you on?' treating a practical question about studying as a loyalty test is very Jeff. Tight construction.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I got half the Spanish exam, which actually helped me with the other half. It's like watching Lost - you don't understand what's happening, but you're invested enough to keep going.

jokes.text: "Does anybody know how to study?" / "Annie usually--" / "Whose side are you on?"
jokes.setup: Jeff rallies the group to study without Annie, then immediately asks who knows how to study
jokes.punchline: The obvious answer is Annie — the person he just banned — which Troy almost says before Jeff cuts him off, refusing to acknowledge the irony
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural comedy: Jeff's rhetorical momentum crashes into the obvious fact he's trying to ignore. His pivot to 'Whose side are you on?' is a great deflection — he weaponizes loyalty to avoid admitting he needs Annie. The beat works because of the buildup to the inevitable (Annie-shaped) answer.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So Professor Escodera, I wanted to thank you for making the midterm so... manageable.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Escodera
dialogue.line: Well Jeff, you studied very hard. I could tell by the way you... applied yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I appreciate that. I mean, some of those questions were almost suspiciously easy.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Escodera
dialogue.line: Perhaps I simply wanted to reward your... dedication to the material. And to me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Right. Well, thanks again for the extra credit opportunity last night.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Escodera
dialogue.line: Anytime, Jeff. My door is always open. As it was last evening.

jokes.text: Dean's PA announcement: nature sounds have continued to 'cut five from sounds of the Serengeti' and now a 'b-side': 'antelope slaughter at Ndutu'
jokes.setup: Dean has been playing relaxing nature sounds for finals week
jokes.punchline: The 'b-side' of his nature sounds album is antelope slaughter — the nature sounds have escalated from babbling brook to wildlife massacre
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the Dean's nature sounds running gag. 'Antelope slaughter at Ndutu' as a 'b-side' is both specific (the proper place name 'Ndutu') and darkly absurd. The joke earns its escalation because we've already accepted the premise twice. This is the running gag's best beat.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Um, I can't wake up Pierce. Is this gonna take an unexpected turn?' Troy: 'You have to know how to do it. Discrimination lawsuit.'
jokes.setup: Pierce won't wake up and they need to rouse him for the exam
jokes.punchline: Troy warns them about waking Pierce in a way that could lead to a discrimination lawsuit — implying Pierce has previously used accusations of discrimination as a weapon when startled
jokes.explanation: Funny Pierce character note — the idea that there's a correct protocol for waking him to avoid a discrimination lawsuit implies a whole history of incidents. 'Preposterous!' from Pierce (presumably half-awake) completing the bit is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Plumber tells Troy: 'I know you could be a plumber.' Troy: 'I'm not gonna be, okay? I'm gonna be sophisticated and have no job...'
jokes.setup: The plumber makes another pitch for plumbing
jokes.punchline: Troy repeats/elaborates his aspiration to be sophisticated and idle — this is the second appearance of this joke, now a running gag
jokes.explanation: The second beat of Troy's plumber rejection. Slightly diminished returns from Joke #35's first appearance, but still character-consistent. The running gag structure works.

jokes.text: Plumber tells Troy: 'For about 10 seconds, from the time I sit down in Spanish to the time I look at your desk — because I think maybe I'll look and he won't be there.'
jokes.setup: Plumber describes the best part of his day, building toward what sounds like it will be a sentimental observation about Troy
jokes.punchline: The 'best part' is the brief window of hope that Troy will be absent — a devastating inversion of the expected mentor speech about cherishing a student
jokes.explanation: Structurally one of the best jokes in the episode. It's a perfect misdirection: the setup mimics the 'you mean the world to me' mentor speech beat-for-beat — specific time reference, emotional build — and then pivots to the opposite meaning. The specificity ('about 10 seconds') makes it feel precise and real. The cold cruelty of 'maybe I'll look and he won't be there' landing after such careful setup earns its score. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it in structural elegance.

jokes.text: Jeff's horoscope-devil exchange with Shirley. Jeff: 'My horoscope predicted suffering.' Shirley: 'No, no. That's good. Horoscopes are the devil trying to trick us.'
jokes.setup: The group reflects on their all-night study session
jokes.punchline: Shirley reframes a prediction of suffering as good news because horoscopes are the devil's deception — her religious framework inverting the logic entirely
jokes.explanation: Shirley's religious worldview being applied to mundane situations is a consistent character note. The logic — 'devil said you'd suffer, so actually you won't' — is perfectly Shirley. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Troy tells Annie: 'He said the best part of his day is when he thinks I won't be there.' Annie: 'Abed, what a terrible thing to say.' Abed: 'It's from a movie.' Annie: 'Well, then the movie it's from is terrible.'
jokes.setup: Troy is hurt by what the plumber said; Annie misattributes the cruelty to Abed
jokes.punchline: Abed clarifies it's from a movie (a known Abed deflection), and Annie's response — 'then the movie it's from is terrible' — treats cinematic worth as an ethical category
jokes.explanation: Annie's 'then the movie it's from is terrible' is a funny, characterful response — she applies moral judgment to cinema based on how it made her feel about Troy. Good ensemble work and callback.

jokes.text: Jeff says 'Tierra del fuego' in the hallway; someone responds 'Uh, I'm friends with Hannah too.' Jeff: 'The whole class is. And you can't have an exam without a class.'
jokes.setup: Jeff apparently shouts random Spanish to rally the class not to take the exam
jokes.punchline: His Spanish phrase ('Tierra del Fuego') is completely wrong for the situation — it means 'Land of Fire,' a region of South America — and yet someone responds as if it makes sense, then Jeff pivots to English for his actual argument
jokes.explanation: Jeff deploying random Spanish to seem in charge is a quick gag that works mainly because of its incongruity. 'Tierra del Fuego' as a rallying cry is funny but doesn't quite land with full impact — the joke is underdeveloped.

jokes.text: The class refuses to take the exam. Dr. Escodera says 'Nooooooo!' — multiple times, including elongated screaming.
jokes.setup: Jeff rallies the class to boycott the exam to save Annie
jokes.punchline: Dr. Escodera's reaction is an extended, increasingly unhinged 'No' — the professional veneer of the strict Spanish professor completely shattering in real time
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that works in context — the teacher's total meltdown is a satisfying reversal — but it's more impact than craft. The repeated 'Nooooooo!' is stock but performed with enough commitment to earn laughs.

jokes.text: Pierce, still apparently asleep or confused, says 'Oh, no! The devil told the truth!'
jokes.setup: Earlier Shirley said horoscopes are the devil lying, implying a prediction of suffering would be false
jokes.punchline: Pierce's exclamation — 'The devil told the truth!' — implies he was listening and panicking about the theological implications
jokes.explanation: A good callback to Shirley's theological framework applied to horoscopes, now paid off by Pierce. His alarm at 'the devil told the truth' is funny because it accepts Shirley's theological premise wholesale and panics about the implications. Well-integrated.

jokes.text: Winger confronts Chang at school; Chang says 'I was showing Annie the magic of electronic sampling' as he plays back his own 'No!' screaming on a sampler keyboard
jokes.setup: Jeff and the group burst in thinking Annie is in danger (after hearing screaming)
jokes.punchline: Chang is enthusiastically looping his own screams as music — having found peace and a creative outlet — the contrast between expected violence and actual music nerdery is total
jokes.explanation: Chang's redemption arc being expressed through electronic music is a funny, specific choice. 'The magic of electronic sampling' as a phrase is very Chang — grandiose about something absurd. The reveal structure works well: screaming heard, violence assumed, music revelation.

jokes.text: Chang's reveal: 'Annie getting me fired was the best thing that ever happened to me.' / He's planning to get his teaching degree and 'maybe get the band back together.'
jokes.setup: Chang was supposedly furious; now he seems transformed and grateful
jokes.punchline: Chang pivots from rage to inspirational life restart with no visible transition — and his vision includes rebooting his key-tar band
jokes.explanation: A callback to Chang's key-tar backstory that also serves as a character resolution. The pivot from murderous rage to 'best thing that ever happened to me' is a quintessential Chang whiplash. The band callback gives it structural satisfaction.

jokes.text: Chang says 'Maybe get the band back together, huh?' — Britta says 'Music lessons would be great for you.' Chang: 'Oh, thanks, Britta.'
jokes.setup: Chang is talking about his music dreams and his key-tar band
jokes.punchline: Britta's 'music lessons would be great for you' is a subtle insult — implying he needs lessons rather than affirming his talent — and Chang takes it as a compliment
jokes.explanation: A quiet, Britta-specific jab — she's slightly condescending but means well — and Chang's warm 'Thanks, Britta' is the character-specific obliviousness. Functions well as a quick closing beat to the Chang subplot.

jokes.text: Post-exam, Jeff tells Annie: 'I treated you like a child for having feelings. Maybe because that's when I stopped having them.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is offering a sincere apology to Annie
jokes.punchline: His self-insight — 'maybe because that's when I stopped having them' — is delivered as an emotional breakthrough but also functions as a devastating self-own that he seems unaware of
jokes.explanation: Jeff's emotional growth is always undercut by his delivery — this functions as both genuine character development and an inadvertent confession that he stopped developing emotionally as a child. Straddles the drama/comedy line well.

jokes.text: Jeff tells Annie: 'You don't have to dress like this to grow up.' Annie: 'You don't like it?' Jeff: 'I was going for more of a professor thing.'
jokes.setup: Annie has changed her outfit to look more mature/professional
jokes.punchline: Jeff calls her a 'travel agent' — implying she missed the mark — and Annie's explanation that she was going for 'professor' is funnier than any look could be
jokes.explanation: 'You look like a travel agent' is a funny specific — not a generic 'you look weird' but a precise, oddly dated profession. Annie's 'I was going for professor' makes it funnier retroactively. Good character-specific exchange.

jokes.text: "What? Why? / What? / Nothing." — group's baffled reaction to the Professor look
jokes.setup: Annie explains she was 'going for a Professor thing'
jokes.punchline: Three overlapping confused reactions ('What? Why? / What? / Nothing.') — the group processes the aspiration and can't engage with it
jokes.explanation: Functional group reaction beat. 'Nothing' as the third response is the best part — someone started to say something and thought better of it. Thin individually but good texture.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I think I nailed it.' Shirley: 'Oh me too. Oh!'
jokes.setup: The group is comparing how they think they did on the exam
jokes.punchline: Pierce and Shirley's mutual confidence is played against the expectation that they were the least prepared — their certainty is funnier given what we know about their study session
jokes.explanation: Light laugh, dependent on performance. Pierce's baseless confidence is a consistent note but this instance is underdeveloped.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Uh, like the first season of The Wire.' / Jeff: 'Exactly the—ah, hell, I can't stay mad at you.'
jokes.setup: The group discusses how the exam was passable despite knowing only some of the material
jokes.punchline: Abed's Wire analogy is so apt that Jeff starts to agree — then pivots to forgiving Annie mid-sentence, suggesting the analogy actually worked emotionally
jokes.explanation: Abed's film/TV reference landing as emotionally functional — not just intellectual — is a great beat. Jeff's interruption of his own agreement to forgive Annie suggests Abed's analogy worked as a reconciliation device. Character-smart writing.

jokes.text: Annie repeats 'Anthropology? Anthropology? Anthropology?' as a callback to the opening scene
jokes.setup: The group needs to plan for next year's class if they all pass Spanish
jokes.punchline: Annie returns to her earlier 'Anthropology?' pitch — escalating to a full group chant — completing the episode's thematic arc while also closing the joke
jokes.explanation: The callback earns its place because it functions both structurally (closing the season arc beat) and comically. The whole group joining the 'Anthropology?' chant, including Abed saying 'I want you to be in my next film' mid-chant, is a funny ensemble beat.

jokes.text: Exam grades are revealed one by one in the study room — escalating tension until Jeff's grade is revealed as 79, preceded by 'I'm sorry, Jeff' — then 80: 'We all pass Spanish!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is getting their grades; the tension builds as Jeff's is last
jokes.punchline: The 'half-hearted mislead' (Jeff apologizing in advance) followed by the reveal of 80 — just barely passing — is played as a fake-out within a fake-out
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-described 'half-hearted mislead' and his apologetic delivery are funnier than the actual reveal. The structure works as a tension/release joke. Dependent on performance.

jokes.text: Characters announcing their exam scores: 68, 81, 95, 70, 85 — then the reveal that Jeff barely passed
jokes.setup: Everyone announces their scores with apparent satisfaction; Jeff's score is held back
jokes.punchline: Jeff's score is 80 — 'we all pass Spanish' — accompanied by Dean's apology for 'the half-hearted mislead,' implying the exam was deliberately made easy by Dr. Escodera
jokes.explanation: The 'half-hearted mislead' acknowledgment from Dean/Dr. Escodera is a nice meta-structural joke about narrative convenience. It's the show acknowledging it needed everyone to pass but doing so in-universe. Satisfying structural comedy.

jokes.text: Final scene: Dean Pelton and Dr. Escodera imply they spent the night together. 'Thanks for making it easy.' 'I was going to say the same to you... but you were gone before breakfast.' 'I'm an early riser.' 'I'll say.'
jokes.setup: Dean thanks Dr. Escodera for making the exam easy (after the class boycotted)
jokes.punchline: The dialogue shifts from professional to clearly sexual — 'you were gone before breakfast' and 'I'm an early riser / I'll say' — revealing a Dean subplot that happened entirely off-screen
jokes.explanation: A perfect final scene joke — the double entendres are layered cleanly over professional language, the reveal happens gradually through the dialogue, and the Dean having a secret romantic subplot with the replacement teacher reframes the exam-made-easy as a personal favor. 'I'll say' as the final line of the episode is well-chosen. High economy.

tmdb_overview: On the eve of an important final exam in Spanish, everyone's grades are jeopardized when it is discovered that Señor Chang has a damaging secret.
insight: Season finale lands 49 jokes in 22 minutes, driven by character chaos over setup-punchline mechanics.
